messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For fifty-six years, Leo had built his life around control—first as a means of survival, later as a professional identity. As a detective, he was the one who pieced together the chaos of other people’s lives, the one who stayed calm while others panicked. But in the quiet of his own mind, he was still the boy who could never predict when the air would turn sharp with burnt cooking oil, sending him back to the small kitchen in his childhood home. That smell could hit him anywhere: in the station break room when someone reheated leftovers, walking past a diner, even in his own apartment if he left a pan on the stove too long. When it came, the memory didn’t creep in gradually—it slammed into him without warning, a full sensory replay of being cornered, of the heat of the stove behind him and the weight of a hand gripping his shoulder. He would be back there, helpless, before he could remind himself he was fifty-six years old and nobody could hurt him now.

The rage that followed was what scared him most. It wasn’t the memory itself—it was the white-hot fury that surged up with it, a fury that felt ancient and bottomless. Leo had learned, over decades, to detach himself from those memories. He would push them into a sealed room in his mind and refuse to open the door. But the detachment had a cost: when he tried to explain what had happened to a therapist years ago, or even to his ex-wife during their marriage, he would lose the thread mid-sentence. The words would scatter, the timeline would blur, and he would fall silent, ashamed that a man who interrogated suspects for a living couldn’t describe his own past.

He had come to believe that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he was—that something inherent in him had drawn the abuse. That belief had only hardened with time. After the divorce, which he attributed to his emotional distance, he added another layer: his reactions since then—the rage, the detachment, the sleeplessness—proved he was a lousy coper. Other people survived childhoods like his and came out functional. He had become a detective, yes, but he was still jumping at shadows. His beliefs about how the world worked had been completely destroyed. There was no justice, no safety, no pattern he could trust. The only pattern he knew was that people who looked like the victims from his childhood—small, quiet, with a particular cast to their eyes—made his stomach clench and his throat tighten. He avoided them without thinking, crossing the street or turning down a different aisle at the grocery store.

His body had become a sentry that never stood down. At night, he had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, even in his own locked apartment. He kept a small knife in his nightstand and checked the windows twice before bed. During the day, he was hypervigilant—scanning rooms for exits, noting the position of every person, every sound. When something reminded him of the stressful experience, his physical reactions were overwhelming: his heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that left him shaky for hours. He had stopped wearing clothes that resembled anything from his childhood—no plaid shirts, no dark blue jackets, nothing that might anchor a memory. He had also stopped seeing people outside of work. Friends had given up inviting him. Colleagues had learned not to ask about his weekends.

What finally brought Leo to seek help was a case. He had been assigned to investigate a series of assaults, and the victims—small, quiet, with that particular look in their eyes—reminded him so acutely of himself that he couldn’t sleep for three nights. During a briefing, a junior officer made an offhand joke, and Leo felt a surge of positive emotion—a brief, disorienting warmth—that terrified him. He didn’t trust positive emotions. They felt like a trap, a prelude to pain. He excused himself from the room and sat in his car, hands trembling, and made an appointment with a psychologist. He was terrified that if he opened the door to those memories, he would never get it closed again. But he was more terrified that he would keep living this way—vigilant, alone, and waiting for the next smell to undo him.
